one_liner: C++-embedded DSL compiling image/array pipelines via LLVM; team's 2013 results beat expert C++, NEON and CUDA 1.1-4.4x.
what_it_does: Halide lets you write an image or array processing pipeline once as pure functions over a grid (the algorithm) and separately say how to compute it (the schedule: tiling, fusion, vectorization, threading, GPU mapping). You build the pipeline with a C++17 API or the Python bindings, then JIT it or compile it ahead of time (generators) to an object file plus a C-ABI header callable from any C/C++ code. It is not a drop-in replacement for an existing C++ function; you rewrite the kernel in Halide and keep a thin call site.
how_it_is_fast: The schedule language makes locality and parallelism trade-offs cheap to explore: compute_at/store_at give producer-consumer fusion, sliding windows and recompute-versus-store choices, split/vectorize/parallel give tiling, SIMD and threading, and gpu_tile maps the same algorithm to CUDA, OpenCL, Metal, Vulkan or D3D12. The compiler infers bounds, lowers to LLVM IR and emits SIMD for SSE/AVX, NEON, HVX and others. Schedules come from an expert or an autoscheduler (Mullapudi2016, Adams2019, Li2018); the wins over hand code come from fused, tiled loop organizations that are too laborious to hand-write, not from better codegen of the same loop nest.
when_to_use: Multi-stage stencil or image pipelines (blurs, pyramids, demosaic, local Laplacian, bilateral grid, resampling) where intermediate buffers kill cache locality in straightforward C++
You need one algorithm to run well on x86 SIMD, ARM NEON, Hexagon HVX and a GPU without maintaining a separate intrinsics or CUDA version per target
Throughput-bound batch or camera processing on multi-megapixel frames where a few ms per frame matters (the team's 2015 slides cite Google HDR+, Photos auto-enhance and Android use)
Teams that can afford an AOT build step (generators) and want a C-ABI static library with no LLVM at runtime
when_not_to_use: General code with data-dependent control flow, pointer-chasing or irregular data structures; Halide covers rectangular array pipelines only
Small one-off kernels where a library call (IPP, OpenCV, BLAS, FFTW) already exists: the project's own slides show BLAS only at parity with Eigen (1x) and the bundled FFT only 1.5x over FFTW
Projects that cannot take an LLVM dependency at build time (the compiler needs LLVM 21-23 at the time of writing; JIT also needs it at runtime)

When nobody will tune schedules: parallelism, vectorization and fusion come only from the schedule (apps/blur spells out .parallel and .vectorize per target), autoscheduler quality varies by pipeline, and its GPU support is labelled experimental (issue #8640)
Latency-critical GPU use measured with the bundled halide_benchmark.h, which its header and issue #2278 warn is misleading for GPU code

integration.form: static lib (AOT generator output: .a/.o plus C-ABI header) or shared lib (libHalide for JIT); pip wheels halide / halide-bin / halide-runtime
integration.dependencies: LLVM (21, 22 or 23, plus clang and lld) to build the compiler; CMake 3.28+; optional Python 3.9+ and pybind11 for bindings; generated AOT pipelines need only the small Halide runtime
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; tested hosts GCC 9.5/11.4, MSVC 2022, AppleClang 14-15
integration.platforms: Targets x86 (SSE/AVX), ARM/AArch64 (NEON), Hexagon HVX, PowerPC, RISC-V, WebAssembly; GPUs via CUDA, OpenCL, Metal, Vulkan, Direct3D 12; hosts Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, QuRT
integration.thread_safety: Not documented in the README; generated pipelines use a shared runtime thread pool sized by HL_NUM_THREADS (default: host core count, max 256)

gotchas: Paper table now attributable from the team's first-party CVPR 2015 tutorial slides (halide/halide.github.com, assets/lectures/Halide_CVPR_intro.pdf): x86 blur 1.2x, bilateral grid 4.4x, camera pipeline 3.4x, 'healing brush' 1.7x, local Laplacian 1.7x; ARM camera pipeline 1.1x; GPU bilateral grid 2.3x, healing brush 5.9x*, local Laplacian 9x*. The record's pairing of 5.9x with bilateral grid is wrong: 5.9x is the asterisked GPU 'healing brush' row, and the asterisked GPU rows compare Halide on a GPU against the CPU expert code (the local Laplacian slide spells out 'GPU: 9x faster (vs. Adobe)', Adobe's code being multi-threaded SSE C++), which is why 5.9x exceeds the abstract's 'up to 5x'.

First-party figures disagree with each other: the same slide deck gives local Laplacian as 1.7x in the results table but '2x faster (vs. Adobe)' (and 20x vs a 300-line reference C++) in the narrative slide; the 2.1x in the record's snippet could not be matched to either.

Harness flaw in the repo's only C++-baseline image app, apps/blur/test.cpp: the 'naive' baseline is a single-threaded scalar loop, and the hand-written SSE/NEON blur_fast uses '#pragma omp parallel for' but the Makefile adds -fopenmp only when $(CXX) is not clang, so on clang/macOS builds the intrinsics baseline runs single-threaded against Halide's .parallel(y) schedule; the program prints three unlabelled times and the output check skips a 64-pixel border.

The paper's expert baselines (hand-tuned camera pipe, Adobe's local Laplacian, IPP-based C++) are not in the repo; apps/local_laplacian, bilateral_grid and camera_pipe now time only manual versus autoscheduled Halide, so no current number against C++ can be reproduced from the repo except apps/fft (single-threaded FFTW_EXHAUSTIVE, 16x16 and 32x32) and cuda_mat_mul (cuBLAS).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Halide over Futhark when the workload is a stencil or image pipeline that must be called from C++ and run well on CPU SIMD, mobile DSPs and GPUs from one source; pick Futhark for general nested data-parallel GPU programs. For a single small FFT or BLAS call, a tuned library (or FFTA.jl in Julia) is simpler, since Halide's own figures show only 1.5x over FFTW and parity with Eigen.
verified_claims_summary: Per the Halide team's 2015 tutorial slides reproducing the PLDI 2013 results (paper PDF itself blocked here), Halide schedules ran 1.2-4.4x faster than expert multi-threaded SSE C++ on a quad-core x86 (bilateral grid 4.4x, camera pipe 3.4x, local Laplacian 1.7x, blur 1.2x), 1.1x faster than the hand-tuned camera pipe on ARM, and 2.3x faster than hand-written CUDA for the bilateral grid; the 5.9x and 9x GPU rows are measured against CPU expert code. CPU models, compilers and flags are not stated in what could be read.
status_note: Very active (last commit 2026-10-09 per the verifier; PyPI release 21.0.0 on 2025-09-16, nightly wheels on pypi.halide-lang.org), MIT-licensed core with apps/bgu under Apache-2.0, used in Google imaging products per the team's slides; evidence remains first-party 2013-2015 figures with the expert baselines absent from the repo.
